title: `batten init --from` prints step 2 twice in the "Next:" list
reason: Reproduced exactly, byte-for-byte, in a fresh sandbox copy of proyecto_ui with my own BATTEN_DB. With --from the "Next:" list emits 1, 2, 2, 3; the control run (bare `batten init` on a separate fresh copy) emits a clean 1, 2, 3, which proves sequential numbering is the intended scheme and that the conditional --from line collides with the line after it. Root cause is visible in cmd/batten/main.go:1472-1478: the ordinals are hardcoded string literals, so `fmt.Printf("  2. reconcile against your prose workflow: %s\n", from)` inside the `if from != ""` branch is followed by an unconditional `fmt.Println("  2. run: batten doctor")`. I specifically checked whether this is one of batten's deliberate looks-like-a-bug behaviours — it is not; fail-open-with-warning, advisory-instead-of-deny, and unmeasurable-instead-of-zero all live in the gate and attribution paths, and nothing in README.md, ROADMAP.md, DESIGN.md, or batten.schema.json describes this output block at all. No test asserts these strings (grep for "reconcile against" and "batten doctor\"" across *_test.go returns nothing), which is consistent with an uncaught typo. The reporter's EXPECTED (1, 2, 3, 4 — the inserted line renumbers the ones after it) is right. Severity is the one thing I would adjust: this is purely cosmetic text in a hint block. No gate, spec generation, DB state, or exit code is affected (exit 0, batten.yaml written correctly in both runs), all four steps are individually correct and actionable, and a user can follow them despite the duplicate label. That is polish, not a functional defect — though there is a fair argument for minor since `init` is the first command a new user ever runs and the tool's value proposition is rigor.

title: `--scan-json` is documented nowhere, yet init's own output tells users to use it
reason:
The three surface observations reproduce exactly, but the finding rests on two false premises and a wrong expectation.

1) "Documented nowhere" is false. The reporter grepped four files (README/ROADMAP/DESIGN/schema), found zero hits, and generalized to "nowhere" — without grepping the one file that both consumes the flag and is named in the very message they quote. A repo-wide grep finds it immediately:
  ./plugin/claude-code/commands/batten-init.md:20:  batten init --scan-json
That is a shipped plugin command file, not an internal note, and the flag gets a dedicated section ("## 1. Get the facts before forming an opinion") explaining what it emits and which four fields matter (harness[], stack[], purpose[], notes[]) — 20+ lines of documentation. (My machine's plugin cache holds a stale 66-line v0.1.0 copy that predates the flag; the current repo file is 113 lines and documents it. Source of truth is the repo.)

2) "init's own output tells users to use it" misreads the sentence. The actual line is: "run /batten-init inside Claude Code instead — it uses `batten init --scan-json`." The imperative is *run /batten-init*; the subject of "it uses" is /batten-init. The clause discloses the mechanism the skill uses — it is not an instruction to the user to type the flag. And /batten-init IS in README.md line 245: "| `/batten-init` | interview the repo (or a prose doc) and write `batten.yaml` |". So the one thing the output actually tells the user to run is documented in exactly the place the reporter says it should be.

3) The EXPECTED behaviour is wrong on the merits. --scan-json is machine-to-machine plumbing, and the source says so at cmd/batten/main.go:1448-1449:
  // --scan-json feeds the facts to /batten-init, which adds the judgment a heuristic can't:
  // mining invariants from AGENTS.md, migrating from a prose doc (--from), naming gates.
I ran it: it writes nothing and dumps raw JSON facts to stdout (early `return nil` at line 1453, before any file write). Listing it in the top-level help beside `--from` would present a JSON dump as a co-equal human option and actively mislead — this is git's plumbing/porcelain split, not a doc gap.

4) The claim that --scan-json is "the richer of the two paths" is backwards. It is strictly *poorer* than plain `batten init`: `batten init` writes a working batten.yaml; `--scan-json` writes nothing at all. The richness comes from the LLM in /batten-init reasoning over the facts, not from the flag.

Separately — and NOT a rescue of this finding — I did hit a real adjacent defect while testing: `batten init --help` does not print help. cmdInit's flag loop (main.go:1431-1440) silently ignores unrecognized args, so `--help` fell through and wrote batten.yaml into my sandbox. That is a genuine unknown-flag-handling bug worth filing on its own, but it is a different problem from the one filed here.

title: `batten init --help` writes batten.yaml instead of printing help; every unknown flag is silently swallowed
reason:
Reproduced exactly, on a fresh copy of the template repo with my own BATTEN_DB, for all three variants the reporter named (`--help`, `-h`, `--bogus-flag`), plus a fourth I added (`--from` with no value). Every one printed the "wrote batten.yaml" banner, exited 0, and left an untracked batten.yaml in the repo.

The source confirms it is not a deliberate behaviour. `cmdInit` at cmd/batten/main.go:1429 parses args with a `switch` that has cases only for `--scan-json` and `--from` and NO default arm, so any other token is dropped on the floor and execution falls straight through to `os.WriteFile(dst, ...)` at line 1460. There is no help path in the function at all.

The reporter's EXPECTED is right, and batten's own code agrees with it: `cmdHookDebug` ends with `return fmt.Errorf("hook-debug: unknown flag %q", args[0])` (cmd/batten/main.go:920). So the "reject unknown flags" convention already exists in this binary — `init` is inconsistent with it, not following a different philosophy. This is not one of batten's deliberate fail-open designs (advisory-instead-of-deny, unmeasurable-instead-of-zero); those are all about attribution under uncertainty, and none of them apply to argument parsing.

Two corrections to the reporter's framing, neither of which rescues the behaviour:

1. Help IS reachable one level up. `batten --help`, `batten help`, and bare `batten` all print the command list — though they exit 2, not 0, which is itself a convention slip. But that usage block only documents `batten init [--from <prose-doc>]`; `--scan-json` appears nowhere in it. So `init --help` is the natural place a user would go looking for the flag that is missing from the top-level help, and it is exactly the place that punishes them with a file write.

2. The blast radius is smaller than "asked for help and got a file" implies. The write is loud (it prints the full path and next steps), non-destructive (a second `batten init` returns `batten: batten.yaml already exists — remove it or edit it by hand`, exit 1), and the file lands untracked (`?? batten.yaml`), so recovery is one `rm`.

I checked whether the swallow generalises to something worse. It does not: `phase --help` and `claim --help` hit their arity checks and error out; `statusline --help` falls through to the harmless sensor path; `close`/`check`/`ingest` skip any `--`-prefixed token but then fail on a missing required argument. `init` is the ONLY subcommand where an unrecognised flag causes a filesystem write. That makes this the sharpest instance of a repo-wide parsing pattern rather than an isolated slip.

Severity: minor. It is real, reproducible, violates a universal CLI convention, and lands on the very first command a new user runs — which is why it sits at the top of minor rather than in polish. But nothing is corrupted, nothing is silently wrong (the tool announces precisely what it did), the enforcement engine is untouched, and recovery is trivial. It is a papercut on the front door, not a broken gate. Not major: no core promise is broken and no user is misled about enforcement state.

title: Skill→domain mapping is prose-substring noise: batten's own plugin skill and an unrelated global UI skill are assigned to the `ml` domain
reason: I could not refute it. In a fresh sandbox copy of proyecto_ui with my own BATTEN_DB, the designated testbed binary (batten-testbed/batten.exe, built 2026-07-27 23:52:58) produced the reported skills lines byte-for-byte, including `skills: [portal-cicd, portal-data-connectors, portal-semantic-layer, portal-synthetic-data, batten-engine, ui-ux-pro-max]` under `ml`. Commit d99b6ef "fix: skill suggestions match a skill's name, never its prose" (2026-07-28T00:07:53, ~15 minutes after the testbed binary was built) implements exactly the reporter's EXPECTED — hyphen-segment match on the skill name, nothing else — and cites the same portal-terraform-gcp and `db` examples. title: init says 'the stack is unknown' and 'NO check command was found' about a repo whose AGENTS.md — which init lists in harness[] — declares the stack and the exact QA gate commands
reason:
The output reproduces verbatim, but the notes are literally true about this repo and the EXPECTED behaviour is the one batten deliberately refuses.

FACT THE REPORTER MISSED: the testbed repo contains ZERO build files and ZERO source files. `find . -not -path "./.git/*" \( -name Makefile -o -name pyproject.toml -o -name package.json -o -name go.mod -o -name requirements.txt -o -name justfile -o -name Taskfile.yml \)` returns nothing; the whole repo is 8 files (6 AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, .gitignore, context/planeacion_proyecto.md). So `make check`, which AGENTS.md documents in a ```bash fence, PROVABLY CANNOT RUN here — there is no Makefile. "NO check command was found" is not a false claim about the repo; it is the correct one.

CONTROL PROVES THE NOTE IS CONDITIONAL, NOT BLANKET: I copied the sandbox, dropped in a real Makefile with lint:/check:/test: targets, and re-scanned. Both notes vanished, `stack` became ["make"], every domain's `check` became ["make lint","make check","make test"] verbatim, and the note flipped to "gates.qa.checks were taken from your build files; confirm they are the right pre-commit checks". The scanner reports what it found, and it found nothing because there is nothing.

THE DESIGN IS EXPLICIT AND DOCUMENTED, IN THREE PLACES:
1. internal/scan/scan.go:366-368 — "deriveStack reports the languages and tooling in play, from marker files that are actually present. It never guesses from a directory name: `ml/` might be Python or it might be Rust, and a spec built on the wrong guess produces `check` commands that do not run."
2. internal/scan/scan.go:126-128 — the literal rationale for the check note: "Only claim the checks came from the build files when some actually did... saying 'taken from your build files' over an empty list is the kind of confident-sounding lie that gets believed."
3. plugin/claude-code/commands/batten-init.md:28-29 — "**`stack[]`** — languages and tooling, from marker files that actually exist. Empty means the repo has no build files yet, NOT that it has no stack." The consumer contract already says exactly what the reporter says is missing.

THE HAND-OFF THE REPORTER CALLS A CONTRADICTION IS THE ARCHITECTURE. scan.go's package doc (lines 1-3): "It reports facts; the judgment (which invariants matter, what a gate should require) is left to the agent or the user." harness[] lists AGENTS.md with the note "the source for invariants no heuristic can derive"; notes[] separately says "mine them from AGENTS.md" and "this repo already has a process (see harness[]) — the spec must agree with it, not replace it"; and batten-init.md:35 orders "read every file in harness[] and purpose[]". init points at AGENTS.md four times in the same payload. Far from claiming AGENTS.md is empty, it is the scan's headline output.

MORE: batten-init.md:50-52 turns the very note under complaint into a scripted interview question — "If `stack[]` is empty or no check was found, say plainly that the gate currently verifies nothing and that it must be filled before `enforcement` moves to `enforce`." The note is working as specified.

THE EXPECTED WOULD BE A REGRESSION. Surfacing "AGENTS.md documents `make check`" as a gate candidate in a repo with no Makefile is precisely the failure mode README.md:232 ("your `check` commands verbatim from your build files ... leaves the rest as explicit TODOs rather than guessing"), batten-init.md:84-85 ("verbatim from the build files (never invented — a check that does not run is worse than no check)"), scan.go:304 ("never invented") and scan.go:411-413 ("`pnpm test` in a repo with a package-lock.json is a check that fails on the first run") exist to prevent. This is the ground rules' named trap: a correct fail-honest design filed as a defect.

RESIDUAL, AND IT IS SMALL: the four-word gloss "the stack is unknown" is looser than the command doc's own careful phrasing, and a human reading scan.json raw (without batten-init.md in context) could momentarily over-read it. The note's first clause already states its exact scope ("no language marker files found"), so this is a wording polish at most, worth maybe changing "the stack is unknown" to "no stack could be derived from them". It does not support the finding as filed, which asserts the notes "are false about the repo" — they are not; they are the only true things that could be said.

3. I also found a symptom the reporter missed: `batten init --from` with the flag as the LAST argument silently swallows it (`i+1 < len(args)` guard falls through with no error), so the user gets a plain init and no indication the flag was dropped. (a) "--from should mine the prose doc" — this expectation is drawn from DESIGN.md §'loom init', which is a pre-rename design doc. (b) "at minimum record it as unit.plan" — already implemented at HEAD, and NOT via --from. Commit 3122d29 ("fix: init reads the backlog for the unit, not just branch names", 2026-07-28 00:04:56) added `unitFromDocs`, which globs `docs/ context/ planning/` for `*plan*`, counts markdown HEADINGS, and fills `UnitName`/`UnitPattern`/`UnitPlan`/`UnitLocator`; `scan.go:586` emits `plan:` into the YAML. (c) "should error when the file does not exist" — CONFIRMED and still valid. Plus the dangling-flag case above.

But nothing is corrupted, no gate falsely passes, no data is lost, the spec fields it would have filled are now filled by the scan anyway, and the real migration path (/batten-init) is documented and functional. Pristine `batten init` output prints `● enforcement: REPORT — gates WARN, they do not block yet.`; deleting one character (`enforcement:` -> `enforcment:`) makes the same doctor print `✓ enforcement: enforce — gates block`, EXIT=0, no warning. Root cause is real and located: internal/spec/spec.go:206 uses gopkg.in/yaml.v3 `yaml.Unmarshal`, which ignores unknown fields; `KnownFields(true)` appears nowhere in the tree, and `Spec.Validate()` checks only values, never the key set. Unknown top-level keys (`bogus_top_level_key: 42`) are likewise accepted silently by both doctor and the runtime loader (`batten phase TASK-001 build` -> `anchor: TASK-001 base SHA = 44630cd`).

The reporter understated it in two ways. (1) It is not a doctor display bug — behaviour changes. With the identical PreToolUse payload for `git commit` on active run TASK-001: with the typo, batten returns `"permissionDecision":"deny"`; after restoring the correct spelling (bogus keys still present), the same payload returns `"systemMessage":"batten (warning — not blocking): ..."` with no deny. One dropped character converts a declared report-mode repo into a hard-blocking one. (2) It generalizes to nested keys in the more dangerous direction: renaming `tokens_per_run` -> `tokens_per_runs` moves `batten budget` from `· tokens 0 / 3.0M [............]` to `no ceilings declared in budget:` while doctor stays green — silently deleting the only tripwire an unattended /batten-night run has.

The EXPECTED behaviour is right, and this is not one of batten's deliberate fail-open designs. batten.schema.json:13 declares `"additionalProperties": false` at the root, so batten itself states that unknown keys are invalid; no executing code path honours it. The documented fail-open is about attribution (hooks.go:283 "cannot attribute this commit to a unit: do not block") and always emits a visible warning; here there is no warning at all, and for `enforcement` the silent failure is fail-CLOSED — stricter than the file declares — which directly defeats the adoption ramp described in spec.go:20-23 and in the init-generated comments. doctor also already implements typo hints for other references (cmd/batten/main.go:1303 prints `(did you mean %q?)` for uninstalled skills/agents), so typo detection is an established doctor responsibility that simply was not applied to spec keys. ROADMAP.md does not list this as a known gap.

The one legitimate counterweight, which is why this is major rather than blocker: README.md:169 says the JSON Schema exists "so your editor completes and validates the file as you type". That is a real mitigation — but nothing batten writes enables it. `batten init` emits no `# yaml-language-server: $schema=` modeline, and neither does the repo's own dogfood batten.yaml nor examples/minimal/batten.yaml, so it only works if the user wires the schema by hand. Nothing is corrupted and the state is recoverable once noticed, so it is not a blocker; but it is silent, trivially triggered, affects the single file that is the product's entire source of truth, and can remove a safety ceiling without a word — clearly above minor. Only correction to the report: `additionalProperties: false` is schema line 13, not 12. Immaterial.

title: `artifacts.handoff` is written into every spec but no phase reads it
reason:
The text reproduces exactly, but the premise behind it is wrong: in batten an artifact is an OUTPUT, and `reads:` is optional consumption. `batten.schema.json` defines `artifacts` as "Where each phase writes its output" — there is no `writes:` key on a phase, so the artifacts map IS the write-target table. The loader enforces the relation in exactly one direction, and I proved both halves in my sandbox: adding `reads: [planning]` to the build phase gives a hard load failure (`✗ ... invalid spec: - phase "build" reads "planning", which is neither an artifact nor a prior phase`), while an artifact with no reader loads clean. The schema states that rationale explicitly ("a phase that reads an artifact nobody writes is a typo"). The reverse is not a typo and is deliberately not flagged.

Every canonical example ships artifacts that no phase reads — including the one the reporter cites. README.md:109-124 declares `planning` AND `resolved`; only `planning` is read. DESIGN.md:100-118 and examples/agrosat/batten.yaml declare five artifacts of which `handoff`, `manual` and `resolved` have no reader. The schema's own `examples` block for `artifacts` is `{planning, resolved}` — one read, one not. Most decisive: batten's own hand-written dogfood spec at $HOME\Proyectos\Public\LoopWorkFlow\batten.yaml:14-25 is the identical shape the reporter filed as a bug — `artifacts: handoff: docs/tasks/{id}.md`, phases build/verify/close, zero `reads:`. The generated draft mirrors the author's own spec on purpose.

`handoff` is in fact consumed. plugin/claude-code/commands/batten-close.md:33-35: "Write the resolution artifact ... To `artifacts[<closing kind>]` with `{id}` substituted." With one artifact declared, that is where the close phase writes — and `close` is the one phase in the draft carrying the hard-gated `requires_verdict: ok`. Drop the "orphan" and the gated phase has no declared destination. Consumption happens agent-side (via the MCP `batten_spec` tool, which exports the artifacts map, internal/mcp/mcp.go:782) rather than in Go, which is the documented division of labour: the binary enforces gates, the agent writes the docs.

Both halves of the EXPECTED are wrong. Wiring `reads: [planning]` into build would require the CLI to invent a `planning` artifact and a `plan` phase this repo never declared — the opposite of init's stated posture (cmd/batten/main.go:1448 reserves prose migration and judgment for the richer `/batten-init` path; the CLI emits only the three mechanically-enforced keys `anchor`/`gate`/`requires_verdict` and never emits `reads:` at all). Wiring `reads: [handoff]` would have build read a doc nothing has written yet. And the fallback ask ("let the note[] say 'declare artifacts when you decide where handoffs live'") is already satisfied, better than proposed: the TODO is inline on the exact line the user must edit (`# TODO: where should per-unit handoffs live?`) rather than 40 lines below in the notes block.

The only legitimate residue is much smaller and in a different file: plugin/claude-code/commands/batten-init.md section 4 lists unit/phases/domains/resources/gates/capabilities/enforcement but omits `artifacts`, so the interview path offers no guidance for resolving that TODO. That is a doc gap worth polish at most, and is not what was filed.

title: Write-set collision deny prints a blank bullet under "Your write-set:" when the trespasser has claimed nothing
reason:
Reproduced verbatim in a fresh sandbox with real hook payloads, and the root cause is exactly as the reporter attributed it.

CONFIRMED BEHAVIOUR. `internal/store/store.go:516-531` (`WriteSet`) builds its result with `var out []string` + `append`, so a node with zero claims yields a **nil** slice. `internal/hooks/hooks.go:448-454` then formats `"Your write-set:\n  %s\n"` with `strings.Join(mine, "\n  ")`, which is `""` for a nil slice. The literal two-space indent in the format string survives, producing a line containing only whitespace. Not a rendering accident on my side — it is in the JSON `permissionDecisionReason` as `...write-set:\n  \nIf this file...`.

NOT A DELIBERATE DESIGN. I specifically checked for the "looks like a bug but is intentional" patterns in this codebase and none apply:
- Fail-open/advisory-vs-deny: irrelevant here. The deny itself is correct and desirable — `agent_id` was present, so the attributed-collision branch (hooks.go:442-455) is the right branch. Only the message body is wrong.
- "Report unmeasurable rather than zero": this principle argues *against* the current output, not for it. Elsewhere the codebase is explicit about empty-state being load-bearing (store.go:536 comments that a nil write-set map "is load-bearing"). This one call site is the place where that care was not applied.
- Documented contract: ROADMAP.md:35 states the guard denies "naming the owner **and B's own write-set**", and README.md:77-83 shows the message only with a populated list. Nothing in README/ROADMAP/DESIGN describes or defends an empty variant.

NOT COVERED BY TESTS. `internal/hooks/guard_test.go:62-86` is the only test of this message, and it claims a write-set for *both* agents before triggering the collision (`ClaimWriteSet(..., "n-b", []string{"api/routes.go"})`), then asserts the reason contains `api/routes.go`. The zero-claim trespasser is an untested path.

REALISTIC, NOT A CORNER CASE. An agent that skipped `batten claim` is precisely the "distracted agent" the guard exists to catch (hooks.go:399-403). The scenario needs only: SubagentStart registered the node, another node owns the file, and this agent never claimed. That is arguably the *most* likely shape of a real trespass.

THE REPORTER'S "EXPECTED" IS DIRECTIONALLY RIGHT, WITH ONE CAVEAT. Replacing the blank bullet with an explicit "you have claimed nothing" line is clearly correct. But the suggested wording — "run `batten claim A2 <file>...`" — must not read as an invitation to claim the *contested* file: `store.go:492` would reject that with `write-set collision: %s is already owned by %s`, and it would contradict the message's own closing line ("fix the plan, do not cross the fence"). The reporter's qualifier "with the write-set from the plan" mostly covers this, but the fix should keep the remedy pointed at the plan, not at the file that was just denied.

SEVERITY. I corrected it to `minor`. Enforcement is fully correct — the deny fires, the file, the owner (`n-A1`) and the trespasser (`n-A2`) are all named, so the agent is not blocked from understanding it trespassed. The damage is confined to one line of guidance: malformed output plus the loss of the most actionable instruction ("you own nothing yet") in the single highest-stakes message batten emits, which matters most in unattended `batten-night` runs where no human reads it. Not `blocker`/`major` — nothing is mis-allowed, mis-denied, or lost. Above pure `polish` because it drops information the ROADMAP explicitly promises and can leave an agent without a recovery path, not merely because it looks untidy.

title: Write-set guard does not look at Bash: an agent denied an Edit can perform the identical write through the shell, silently
reason:
REPRODUCED EXACTLY, in a fresh sandbox with my own BATTEN_DB. This is not a case of a deliberate design being misread as a bug — I checked the three places where batten documents its intentional fail-opens, and this one is not among them.

WHAT I CONFIRMED

1. The behaviour. `batten claim A1 backend/app/main.py`, then A2 attempts the same file:
   - via Edit -> `permissionDecision":"deny"` with the full collision message.
   - via Bash (`echo ... > backend/app/main.py`, `sed -i`, `cp`, `tee`, and the reporter's python heredoc) -> empty output on all five, exit 0. No deny, no warning, no additionalContext.
   I then executed the write for real. A1's claimed file was clobbered end to end.

2. The cause, in source. `internal/hooks/hooks.go:248-264` — `preToolUse` switches on tool name: `Bash` goes to `verdictGate` only, `Write|Edit|NotebookEdit` go to `writeSetGuard`. `verdictGate` (line 271-274) returns immediately unless `commitRe` matches. The command string is never tested against claimed paths. The reporter is right that the payload reaches the binary: `plugin/claude-code/hooks/hooks.json` matches Bash on PreToolUse, and I verified the binary parses that payload fine.

3. It is silent after the fact too. `postToolUse` fires on Bash but only handles `batten phase` session-binding and commit-close; I ran it against the offending command and got empty output. Worse, `batten show US-001` afterwards still prints `[subagent] backend  running  owns 1 file(s)` — the run record keeps asserting an ownership that was already violated.

WHY THIS IS NOT ONE OF BATTEN'S DELIBERATE FAIL-OPENS

I looked for the "correct design filed as a defect" pattern and it is absent:
- Principle #3 (ROADMAP.md:198) is "Fail open only out loud. If the gate cannot attribute the work, it does not block — and it says so." That principle governs *attribution failure*. Here attribution is complete: agent_id present, node resolved, run resolved, path claimed. batten simply never asks the question.
- Every other deliberate fail-open in this file is justified by an in-place comment: the unattributed-write advisory (hooks.go:436-447, "the risks are asymmetric"), the no-checks gate advisory (hooks.go:337-350, "it passes OUT LOUD"), ambiguous-unit silence (hooks.go:667). There is no comment at the Bash branch acknowledging shell writes. In a codebase that argues with itself in comments this consistently, the silence is evidence it was not considered.
- No test pins it: `internal/hooks/guard_test.go` contains no occurrence of "Bash".
- DESIGN.md:238 and :294 do scope the guard to matcher `Write|Edit`, but they scope it to the tools that carry a `file_path` — they never discuss Bash as a write vector, so this is the mechanism being described, not a threat being dismissed.

The sharpest point, which is why I could not refute this: batten's founding thesis (ROADMAP.md:20-24) is that "prose cannot stop a git commit" — hooks exist precisely because the agent's cooperation cannot be assumed. The only thing currently standing between a denied agent and the identical write is a sentence inside the denial ("fix the plan, do not cross the fence"). Closing this hole with prose is the exact move batten was built to reject.

WHERE THE REPORTER IS WRONG

The EXPECTED direction is right — a warning, not a deny, is correctly calibrated and consistent with the project's ramp. But the proposed remedy is the weaker of two available ones. A PreToolUse regex over `>`/`>>`/`tee`/`sed -i`/`mv`/`cp` catches literal-path cases and is blind to the far more common tool-invocation cases: `prettier --write .`, `black .`, `make`, `npm run codegen`, any script. That converts "no coverage" into "partial coverage that reads as complete", which is its own hazard for a fence. The better mechanism already has its plumbing installed: PostToolUse:Bash fires today. Hashing or stat-ing the (small, declared) set of claimed paths not owned by this agent, before and after a Bash call, is decidable, has no shell-parsing false negatives, and warns on the ones a regex can never see. Detection after the fact is weaker than prevention, but complete detection beats partial prevention here.

SEVERITY: minor, and I think that is honest rather than generous. It is "missing", not "broken" — the Edit/Write path does exactly what it is documented to do, and ROADMAP's Verified claim ("Agent B editing agent A's file -> DENY") is literally true. Triggering it needs an active fan-out with claims plus an agent choosing a shell to write a file, the consequence is a clobbered file rather than a breached security boundary, and the verify phase's `diff_from: anchor` still surfaces the change (just not who made it). It is not a blocker and batten is not worse than its absence. What keeps it above "polish" is that it sits in one of the two headline wedges, and the guard's own denial is a plausible trigger for the uncovered path.

title: Three ordinary spellings of `git commit` walk straight through the verdict gate
reason: Reproduced exactly in a fresh sandbox with my own BATTEN_DB. `git -C . commit -m x`, `git -c user.email=a@b.c commit -m x` and `git.exe commit -m x` are all ALLOWED (empty hook output) under the identical session/cwd/DB where plain `git commit -m x` is DENIED. Root cause is one regex at internal/hooks/hooks.go:267 — `(^|[;&|]|\s)git\s+(-[^\s]+\s+)*commit\b`. The flag group only consumes options whose value is glued on (`--git-dir=.git` is correctly denied); any global option taking a SEPARATE argument (`-C <dir>`, `-c <k=v>`) ends the group at the value token, so `commit` is no longer where the pattern expects it. `git\s+` also cannot match `git.exe`. This is not one of batten's deliberate fail-opens: attribution succeeds here (form A denies with the same input), so the hooks.go:281 "cannot attribute -> do not block" path is never reached; the gate simply fails to recognise the command. The reporter's EXPECTED matches the project's own stated contract, not merely their taste — DESIGN.md:383 says "Un `git commit` sin evidencia **es imposible**" and ROADMAP.md:34 says "`git commit` without a verdict -> DENY". Two further points confirm oversight rather than intent: (1) the sibling regex 24 lines earlier, `phaseRe = \bbatten(?:\.exe)?\s+phase\s+(\S+)`, explicitly handles the `.exe` spelling for batten's own binary but not for git, on a Windows-first project; (2) the same `commitRe` is the run-closer in postToolUse (hooks.go:223), and I confirmed a `git -c ... commit` PostToolUse leaves the run `running` while plain `git commit` flips it to `ok` — so the miss both opens the gate and strands the run holding its write-set claims. But these are ordinary non-adversarial spellings (`-c user.email=` is the standard non-interactive form, `-C <dir>` is used from anywhere but the repo root, `git.exe` is the literal Windows name) and they defeat the product's central guarantee silently, without the audit record that `batten override` exists to produce. One cosmetic discrepancy from the report: the reporter's deny text was "has no batten-verified pass..." while mine was "has no verdict envelope..." — a different branch of the same deny, reflecting that they had a recorded-but-unverified verdict. title: Phase nodes have globally-unique ids (`p-<phase>`), so any run entering a phase steals that node from every other run — silently emptying their DAGs, canvases and MCP graphs, across units AND across projects
reason:
CONFIRMED, byte-for-byte, and the reporter understated it.

REPRODUCTION (fresh sandbox, own BATTEN_DB, own copy of proyecto_ui). BEFORE was identical to the report — `show US-012` listed `[phase] build` + `[subagent] backend`, canvas "4 nodes, 1 edges". After a single `batten phase US-013 build`, `show US-012` lost its phase node and the canvas dropped to "1 nodes, 0 edges". Re-running `batten phase US-012 build` ping-ponged it back (US-012 4 nodes, US-013 1 node). Every claim in the report reproduced.

THE MECHANISM IS EXACTLY AS DIAGNOSED. `internal/store/store.go:84` declares `node_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY` — the id alone, not `(run_id, node_id)` — and `AddNode` (store.go:397-409) is `INSERT OR REPLACE`. `cmdPhase` (cmd/batten/main.go:367-369) builds `NodeID: "p-" + phaseID`, which contains no run. So the whole database holds exactly ONE row per phase name, forever. A direct dump of my DB after four runs proves it:
  NODES: ('n-C1', 'US-012-…', 'subagent', …), ('p-build', 'US-021-…', 'phase', …)
Four runs, four `batten phase … build` calls, one surviving `p-build` row. Three runs' phase nodes were destroyed, not orphaned — the UPDATE-in-place moved the single row.

THE EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR IS RIGHT, AND THIS IS NOT ONE OF BATTEN'S DELIBERATE FAIL-OPEN DESIGNS. I checked for that specifically. The fail-open behaviours are advertised and visible: unattributed writes are advisory, unmeasurable ceilings report NOT MEASURABLE, and ambiguous attribution refuses to guess (I hit that one live — a SubagentStart fired while two runs were open created no node at all, correctly and by design). This is the opposite: silent, permanent destruction with no warning on any surface. `nodes` has a `run_id` FK and `Store.Nodes(runID)` filters by run, so per-run graphs are plainly the intent; the PK is simply wrong. README:260 "The run graph … draws the path the work **actually took**" and ROADMAP's "Multi-session — verified" are both contradicted.

THREE AMPLIFICATIONS THE REPORTER DID NOT FIND:

1. It is not only the phase node that vanishes — the subagents vanish too. `canvas.Render` (internal/canvas/canvas.go:117-124) buckets children by `parent[nodeID]`, and its orphan column only catches `parent == ""`. n-C1's parent is still `"p-build"`, which is no longer in this run, so the subagent is silently dropped — the exact outcome the code comment "so nothing is silently dropped" promises against. That is why the canvas is 1 node (bare header), not 3.

2. It crosses projects, not just units. `dbPath()` (main.go:128-137) is one `~/.batten/batten.db` per USER. I created a second repo with `project: otro-proyecto`, ran `batten phase US-500 build` against the same DB, and portal-datos' US-021 canvas went to "1 nodes, 0 edges". An unrelated repo empties your run graph.

3. It corrupts closed history irreversibly. `batten close US-020 --status rolled_back` → archived canvas "3 nodes, 0 edges". Then one unrelated `batten phase US-021 build` → the archived, rolled-back, finished US-020 exports "1 nodes, 0 edges". A CloseRun does not protect the record.

The MCP surface the agent itself reads is left internally inconsistent, not merely empty: `batten_run_graph {"unit":"US-012"}` returns `"edges":[{"from":"p-build","to":"n-C1"}]` with `p-build` absent from `nodes`. A dangling edge handed to the model.

Why no test caught it: every test touching `p-build` (canvas_test, export_test, graph_test, tui_test) uses a single run, so the collision is never exercised.

SEVERITY — blocker, honestly argued. Against: the enforcement rails are untouched. I verified the write-set guard keys on `PRIMARY KEY (run_id, path)` and verdicts on `run_id`, so no false ALLOW and no false DENY result from this; a reader who weighs gates above the record could defend "major". For: batten's own pitch is "procedural memory as data", the run graph is the artifact, the damage is silent, permanent, guaranteed by the second work item in any repo, and unavoidable without one DB per unit — which would itself disable the cross-run guard. The README's headline `batten canvas` demo produces an empty file for every unit but the newest.

Fix shape: PK on `(run_id, node_id)`, or namespace the id with the run — but edges, `FinishNode` and `NodeByAgent` all key on `node_id` alone and must move together. Note `n-` + AgentID (hooks.go:479) has the same latent shape; agent ids are usually session-unique, so I did not reproduce a collision there, but nothing in the schema prevents one.

title: `batten claim` has no cross-run check: two open runs are each told they own the same file, then both are denied on it (and the MCP advisor tells both they may write)
reason:
Reproduced exactly, in a pristine sandbox, and confirmed in the source. This is a real gap, not a deliberate fail-open.

WHAT THE CODE SAYS. `Store.ClaimWriteSet` (internal/store/store.go:481-503) checks for an existing owner with `SELECT node_id FROM writesets WHERE run_id=? AND path=?` — scoped to one run. Its own comment states the guarantee it believes it provides: "The PRIMARY KEY (run_id, path) means the database itself refuses a second owner for a file — the disjointness rule is not advice, it is a constraint." That constraint is per-run only. The cross-run defense (`WriteSetOwnerAcrossOpenRuns`, store.go:1062) exists and works, but is called only from `writeSetGuard` at PreToolUse (internal/hooks/hooks.go:459). So claim-time and write-time disagree about the scope of the invariant: claim enforces per-run, the hook enforces per-project-open-runs. Nothing reconciles them.

WHY IT DEADLOCKS BOTH. In `writeSetGuard`, the within-run check passes for a declared owner (owner == myNode), so control falls through to the cross-run check, which finds the *other* run's claim. Symmetric for both agents. Denying both is the safe direction, but it is only reachable because claim accepted a claim it should have questioned.

THE DEFECT IS BATTEN VIOLATING ITS OWN STATED RULES, NOT ME MISREADING A DESIGN:
- ROADMAP.md "Verified" table asserts: "Multi-session | Session↔run binding; write-sets defended *between* open runs". Here the between-open-runs rule is enforced only after the plan is already broken, and enforced against the very agents batten recorded as owners.
- ROADMAP.md "Principles that do not bend" #3: "Fail open only out loud." The second claim fails open (rc=0) and is not out loud — it prints a reassurance.
- The success line is factually false in this state: `B1 owns 1 file(s); any other agent writing them is now denied` — in fact B1 itself is denied.
- plugin/claude-code/commands/batten-build.md §5 ("When a claim collides, THE PLAN IS WRONG") explicitly names `batten claim` reporting a collision as one of the two places this is supposed to surface. It does not surface here.
- The double-claim case is untested: internal/store/lifecycle_test.go has TestWriteSetRefusesASecondOwner (single run) and TestCrossRunGuardOnlyDefendsOpenRuns (one claimant, two runs). No test ever claims one path in two open runs. This is a hole, not a decision.

ONE THING I FOUND THAT THE REPORT MISSED, which makes it worse. `mcp.batten_writeset_owner` — the tool the MCP server instructions tell agents to call "Before writing a file as a fanned-out subagent" — also only consults the caller's own run (mcp.go:681, `q.st.WriteSetOwner(r.RunID, rel)`). In the deadlocked state it returns, for BOTH agents, `"owned_by_you": true, "write_allowed": true`. The advisory tool and the enforcing hook flatly contradict each other, so an agent that follows the documented pre-flight check is told it is clear and is then denied anyway.

WHERE THE REPORTER IS PARTLY WRONG (does not refute the finding, but the EXPECTED needs correcting). The proposed message `write-set collision: ... is already owned by US-010 (run ...)` does not match batten's real in-run wording, which names the node, not the unit — I confirmed the control case prints `batten: write-set collision: backend/app/main.py is already owned by n-A1`, rc=1. More substantively, a cross-run collision is a *different* problem from an in-run one: in-run means one plan with an overlap ("fix the plan"), cross-run means two independently planned units in two sessions, for which batten's own prescribed remedy is different ("Coordinate, or use a worktree per unit"). So the fix is not to reuse the in-run text at claim time; it is a distinct cross-run failure (or at minimum a loud warning) at claim time carrying the worktree/coordination remedy. The reporter's core claim — that the collision must surface at claim time instead of detonating later — is right.

ALSO CORRECTING THE REPORT ON "DEADLOCK". It is not permanent. I verified the exit: `batten close US-011 --status failed` prints "Write-set claims released — files it held are free again" and A1's edit is then allowed. But nothing tells a user that: the deny message never mentions that the caller is itself a recorded owner, `batten doctor` reports nothing about two open runs claiming one path, and `batten show US-010` cheerfully prints "owns 1 file(s)". So it is a recoverable stall with an actively misleading diagnosis, not a brick.

SEVERITY. Not a blocker: it fails safe (deny, never a silent double-write), there is no data loss, and it is fully recoverable by closing a run. Not minor either: multi-session write-set defense is an advertised, "Verified" capability; the state is reachable through the normal skill-driven flow with no hand-driving (two sessions, two units, one shared module such as a router or app entrypoint — exactly `backend/app/main.py` in the test repo); the outcome hard-blocks both fan-outs; and three separate surfaces (claim's success line, the MCP advisor, the deny message) each state something untrue or incomplete about it. reason:

Case B (run_id = the caller's own US-002 run) — identical:
  {"note":"unclaimed: no agent owns this file in run US-002-...","owned":false,"write_allowed":true}
The guard on that exact write, both with and without `agent_id` in the payload:
  {"hookSpecificOutput":{"permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"batten: ml/pipelines/eda.py is being worked by US-004 in another open session (run US-004-...)"}}

WHY IT IS NOT A DELIBERATE DESIGN
1. The tool's own contract is "predict the gate", not "answer a narrower question". `internal/mcp/mcp.go:635` documents the field as `"false means a Write/Edit here would be DENIED by the write-set guard"`; the tool description (mcp.go:110-113) says "if another agent owns it, the PreToolUse hook will DENY your Write/Edit"; the server Instructions say "Before writing a file as a fanned-out subagent call batten_writeset_owner." The cross-run check the tool omits (`WriteSetOwnerAcrossOpenRuns`, hooks.go:459) lives inside `writeSetGuard` itself — it IS the write-set guard, so there is no "different mechanism" defence.
2. The refusal-to-guess in `resolveRun` (mcp.go:840-904) is deliberate and correct for budget/verdict attribution — but `agent_id` is not a guess. `NodeByAgent` (store.go:418) returns a single deterministic row with its `run_id`; `writeSetOwner` already calls it at mcp.go:670, just *after* `resolveRun` has already bailed. The hook does exactly the right thing at hooks.go:420-424 (agent_id first, then session/unit).
3. Even accepting the refusal to resolve, `write_allowed` is initialised `true` at mcp.go:642 and never reset, so an unresolvable run yields a definite green light. That contradicts batten's own stated principle — ROADMAP.md:195 "Never invent a number. What cannot be measured is reported as unmeasurable", and the sibling tool `batten_budget` which is documented as "A ceiling that cannot be measured is reported as unavailable with the reason — never as zero." The reporter's `write_allowed: null`/unknown is the same pattern batten already applies elsewhere.
4. The code comment at mcp.go:700-702 ("the guard keys off agent_id, so the orchestrator (which has none) is never denied. Reporting otherwise would be a lie") is stale: it is true within a run, false across runs. I denied the orchestrator (no agent_id, session B main loop) on the cross-run path.

- Case A is broader than "cross-run". With 3 runs open I asked agent-be-4 about `frontend/src/App.tsx`, owned by agent-fe-2 *inside agent-be-4's own run US-002*: tool says `write_allowed: true`, hook says "write-set collision ... belongs to another agent's write-set (n-agent-fe-2); you are n-agent-be-4". - The note's escape hatch does not exist. With `run_id` supplied and the collision inside that run, the tool agrees with the hook exactly: `write_allowed: false`, `owner_agent_id: agent-fe-2`, same wording as the deny. The defect is confined to the two resolution gaps (agent_id ignored for run resolution; no cross-run check), not to the tool as a whole.

title: `batten claim` accepts directories, globs and out-of-repo paths, printing "any other agent writing them is now denied" for a claim that can never match
reason:
Reproduced exactly, in a fresh sandbox with my own BATTEN_DB, including both halves of the report plus a third case the reporter did not test.

`batten claim agent-fe-4 <repo>/frontend/` printed `agent-fe-4 owns 1 file(s); any other agent writing them is now denied` (rc=0), and the very next `hook PreToolUse` for `agent-be-4` editing `<repo>/frontend/pages/index.vue` returned empty output, rc=0 — ALLOWED. Same for `batten claim agent-fe-4 C:/Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts` (accepted, "owns 1 file(s)", and a subsequent Edit of that exact path is ALLOWED). I additionally tested `batten claim agent-fe-4 <repo>/frontend/**`, which is also accepted with the same sentence and also fences nothing: an Edit of `frontend/components/Foo.vue` by another agent was ALLOWED.

Dumping the DB shows why — the rows are stored verbatim and matching is exact string equality:
  ('n-agent-fe-4', 'frontend')
  ('n-agent-fe-4', 'frontend/pages/index.vue')
  ('n-agent-fe-4', 'c:/windows/system32/drivers/etc/hosts')
  ('n-agent-fe-4', 'frontend/**')
Only the second row can ever be hit. `batten show US-010` compounds it: "[subagent] frontend  running  owns 4 file(s)" — three of those four protect nothing.

The reporter's mechanism is accurate. `cmdClaim` (cmd/batten/main.go:322) only rewrites to a repo-relative path when `filepath.Rel` succeeds AND the result does not start with ".."; otherwise it stores the absolute path. `writeSetGuard` (internal/hooks/hooks.go:408-415) always computes `filepath.Rel(Spec.Root, path)` and returns nil (allow) for anything starting with "../", so an out-of-repo claim is unreachable by construction. `Store.WriteSetOwner` / `WriteSetOwnerAcrossOpenRuns` are plain `WHERE path=?` equality — no directory-prefix or glob semantics exist anywhere.

This is NOT one of batten's deliberate look-like-a-bug behaviours. It is not fail-open-with-a-warning (no warning is printed), not advisory-instead-of-deny (no advisory is emitted), and not unmeasurable-instead-of-zero (it reports a positive guarantee, not an unknown). It is the exact inverse of the project's own stated ethic: ROADMAP.md opens with "If a hook cannot enforce it or a command cannot run it, it does not go in batten.yaml", and lists as a verified virtue "An unmeasurable ceiling reports NOT MEASURABLE, never a fabricated zero". Here the command fabricates an enforcement guarantee it does not have, in the mechanism ROADMAP.md advertises as "a database constraint, not advice".

The EXPECTED behaviour is right in substance. Two refinements: (a) the fix must NOT be "the file must exist" — claiming a file an agent is about to create is legitimate and works today; the checks that are actually missing are "this path is an existing directory", "this path contains glob metacharacters", and "this path escapes the repo root". (b) The reporter's title over-reaches slightly: the write-set guard itself is sound. My control test confirms `batten claim a1 frontend/pages/index.vue` (relative, from repo root, as /batten-build documents) followed by another agent's Edit produces a correct DENY naming the owner, both within a run and across open runs. So it is `batten claim` failing to validate its arguments, not the guard failing to enforce — I have retitled accordingly.

Two things make this more than pedantry rather than pure user error. First, the plugin's own /batten-plan template writes write-sets in glob and ellipsis form — `write-set: <dir>/features/*.py, tests/<dir>/features/...` — and /batten-build then says to feed that write-set straight to `batten claim`. On Windows (the platform batten specifically claims verified hook support on) native arguments are not shell-expanded, so a build agent following the plugin's own documents verbatim lands on the silent-no-op path. Second, `cmd/batten` sits at 8% test coverage by ROADMAP.md's own table, and nothing in ROADMAP.md's "Not built" or "Open questions" sections acknowledges this gap, so it is not a knowingly deferred item.

Severity: major, not blocker. The documented happy path (a list of real file paths) enforces correctly, nothing is corrupted, and no run is stopped. But a headline safety mechanism silently degrading to nothing while printing an explicit assurance to the contrary is precisely the false-confidence failure batten exists to eliminate, and the operator has no signal that the fence is empty.

title: A relative `file_path` in the tool payload silently bypasses the write-set guard
reason:
Reproduced exactly as described in a fresh sandbox, and the reporter's root-cause diagnosis is correct.

CONFIRMED MECHANISM. `writeSetGuard` (internal/hooks/hooks.go:404-415) does `rel, err := filepath.Rel(h.Spec.Root, path)` and on `err != nil` returns `nil, nil` — allow, with no output at all. `filepath.Rel` errors whenever the base is absolute and the target is relative. Go probe (go1.26.3):
  Rel(`$HOME\sandbox\repo`, "ml/pipelines/eda.py") => err=Rel: can't make ml/pipelines/eda.py relative to $HOME\sandbox\repo
The whole guard is skipped: within-run collision AND cross-run collision.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE REPORTER. This is NOT Windows-specific. The same probe with a POSIX root fails identically:
  Rel("$HOME/repo", "ml/pipelines/eda.py") => err=Rel: can't make ml/pipelines/eda.py relative to $HOME/repo
`filepath.Rel` rejects mixed absolute/relative on every platform. The bug bites Linux and macOS the same way. The reporter's "on Windows" framing understates the scope.

IS THE EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR RIGHT? Yes, and I checked the three deliberate-fail-open designs before concluding this.
1. It is not the documented "outside the repo" carve-out. That branch is the `strings.HasPrefix(rel, "../")` check on the next line, and it carries an explicit comment. The `err != nil` branch has no comment — it is bare defensive code, not stated intent.
2. It is not the "cannot attribute" fail-open. batten attributes this write perfectly: it has `agent_id` (agent-be-4 resolves to node n-agent-be-4) and it has `cwd` in the payload. It already uses `in.CWD` for exactly this kind of resolution in `activeUnit` (hooks.go:635). Nothing is unknown; the path is simply not resolved.
3. Most decisively, it violates batten's own stated non-bending principle. ROADMAP.md:198 — "Fail open only out loud. If the gate cannot attribute the work, it does not block — and it says so." This fail-open is silent: empty stdout, no `systemMessage`, no `additionalContext`, exit 0. Even the most generous reading of batten's philosophy requires an `advise(...)` here, not silence.

REACHABILITY (why this is not theoretical). The tool layer does not reject relative paths — it resolves them against cwd. I verified this in this very session: `Read` with `file_path: "README.md"` returned the file, and `Write` with `file_path: "../../../AppData/.../refute-relpath/relwrite-proof.txt"` returned "File created successfully" and the file exists on disk (33 bytes). So a model that emits a relative path gets a real write, and batten says nothing. The schema says "absolute", so this is uncommon rather than routine — the two real payloads in ~/.batten/hook-taps.jsonl are both absolute — but "uncommon" is precisely the failure mode batten exists to catch.

SCOPE — the guard is otherwise sound. I characterized six other path shapes against the same claimed file; only the relative forms leak:
  abs forward-slash        -> deny
  abs Windows backslash    -> deny   (the form real Claude Code emits)
  abs containing ..        -> deny
  lowercase drive letter   -> deny
  relative                 -> ALLOWED (empty)
  ./relative               -> ALLOWED (empty)
  relative backslash       -> ALLOWED (empty)

TEST GAP. internal/hooks/guard_test.go:35-36 — `writeInputFor` builds every payload as `filepath.Join(root, rel)`, so every guard test is absolute, and the fixture `Input` never sets `CWD`. Nothing in the suite could have caught this.

SEVERITY: major, not blocker. Not a blocker because the overwhelmingly common absolute form is denied correctly, so a normal fan-out is genuinely fenced — the guard is not broken in general. Not minor because when it does fire it silently defeats one of batten's two headline wedges ("the fence is the feature", README.md:68-92), delivering exactly the merge-time surprise batten was built to prevent, with zero signal to the user or the model, and because it contradicts a principle the project declares does not bend. The fix is small: resolve `path` against `in.CWD` (falling back to `h.Spec.Root`) before `filepath.Rel`, and make the residual error path `advise(...)` rather than silence.

title: A commit for an attributable unit with no recorded run is allowed in total silence
reason:
The OBSERVED behaviour reproduces byte-for-byte, but the finding's premise ("in total silence") is false at the system level, and the EXPECTED is wrong: this is a deliberate, in-source-documented, unit-tested design with an explicit compensating disclosure.

1) It is deliberate and labelled as such. internal/hooks/hooks.go:284-287:
   run, err := h.Store.ActiveRun(h.Spec.Project, unit)
   if err != nil {
       return nil, nil // no run recorded: the gate has nothing to say
   }
The reporter is right about the mechanics — activeUnit() DOES resolve US-011 from the branch (hooks.go:639-647), so the bail is not the unattributable path at line 281. But batten's unit of governance is the run, not the branch: with no run there is no anchor SHA, no phase, no write-set, no diff_from, and no ledger. There is nothing to gate.

2) It is NOT silent. batten states this case explicitly on the surface its own MCP server instructs the agent to consult before committing ("Before committing a work item call batten_verdict_status"). I ran that server against my sandbox DB and got:
   "how_to_fix":"no run is recorded, so the gate has nothing to enforce and will not block a commit. That is not an approval: nothing has been verified."
   "note":"no run has been recorded for US-011", "commit_denied":false
That string exists precisely to prevent the reading the finding makes. It is pinned by a test — internal/mcp/mcp_test.go:663-667 asserts commit_denied==false with the comment "with no run recorded the hook cannot attribute a commit, so it does not block", and then fails the build if how_to_fix does not contain "not an approval", with the rationale "silence here reads as approval, which it is not". The exact concern the reporter raises is already a regression test.

3) The gate is not weak — it is un-armed. The instant the omitted setup step runs, the gate bites hard, with no other change:
   $ batten phase US-011 build   -> anchor: US-011 base SHA = 44630cd
   $ batten hook PreToolUse < payload.json
   {"hookSpecificOutput":{"permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"batten: US-011 has no verdict envelope. Run the \"verify\" phase before committing. ..."}}
So this is not a hole in the gate; it is the gate correctly scoping itself to work batten was actually asked to govern.

4) The proposed fix has a real, reproducible false-positive cost on the identical code path. ActiveRun filters status='running', so a CLOSED unit hits the same branch. I closed US-011 and re-ran the same payload: [hook exit=0], silence. A warning at line 286 would therefore nag on every follow-up commit, --amend, or fixup after a unit was legitimately verified and closed — training users to ignore batten, which is the failure mode ROADMAP.md:341-346 explicitly reasons about elsewhere ("refusing every commit in a repo that has not declared its checks yet would just get batten uninstalled").

5) Principle 3 (ROADMAP.md:198) is "Fail open only out loud. If the gate cannot attribute the work, it does not block — and it says so." This is not that case: nothing was attributed wrongly and nothing was silently degraded from a promised check — no check was ever requested.

Honest residual, stated as the enhancement it is rather than the defect it was filed as: the disclosure lives only on the MCP surface, which an agent that skipped `batten phase` is exactly the agent least likely to call, and SessionStart is silent too (sessionStart returns nil when ListRuns is empty, hooks.go:565-567 — verified: SessionStart on this branch with an empty DB printed nothing). A one-line advise() when LatestRun (not ActiveRun) finds no run at all for a branch-named unit would close that without the fixup-nagging cost of the reporter's version. That is a polish-grade improvement to a working design, not a defect, and certainly not a gate that "allows a commit in total silence".

title: `batten check` exits 0 when the gate is BLOCKED
reason:
Reproduced exactly in a fresh sandbox. `batten check US-011` printed `US-011: BLOCKED (batten-verified). one or more gate checks failed` and exited 0, and `batten.exe check US-011 >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo 'gate green'` printed `gate green`.

The stronger version of the finding, which the reporter did not state: the exit code carries **zero** information in either direction. Same command, same unit, back to back — BLOCKED -> exit 0, OK -> exit 0. It is a constant. And there is no machine-readable fallback: `batten check US-011 --json` silently ignores the flag (no error, no JSON), and `batten show US-011 --json` likewise prints human text and exits 0. The only programmatic way to learn a gate verdict from the CLI is grepping emoji-decorated prose for the word BLOCKED.

I checked the three ways this could have been a correct design filed as a defect, and none hold:

1. **Not a fail-open.** batten's deliberate fail-open behaviours are about *uncertainty* — it cannot attribute a write, so it warns and allows; a gate declares no checks, so it passes rather than refusing every commit in an unconfigured repo. Both of those branches carry explicit explanatory comments in `internal/hooks/hooks.go:337-341`. Here batten has total certainty: it shelled out, watched the command exit 1, and recorded `result = "blocked"`. `cmd/batten/main.go:786-803` sets `result := "blocked"` and then falls through to a bare `return nil` with no comment — in a codebase that comments every counterintuitive branch, that silence is evidence it was not a decision.

2. **It contradicts batten's own convention.** `batten close US-011 --status ok` against the same blocked verdict exits **1**: `batten: cannot close US-011 as ok: needs a verdict with result=ok and cited evidence`. So sibling commands do signal bad state via exit code. `check` is the outlier.

3. **The product actively points users at this command.** The PreToolUse deny message (`internal/hooks/hooks.go:331-335`) tells the user `Run: batten check <unit>`. Composing that instruction the obvious way — `batten check US-011 && git commit …` — yields a false green.

Where the reporter overreached: they framed this as the gate failing ("WRONG: the gate is BLOCKED"), which reads as a bypass. It is not. I drove the full commit path and the enforcement held — after the blocked check, `batten hook PreToolUse` on `git commit` returned `permissionDecision: "deny"` with `batten: US-011 verdict is "blocked", not "ok"`. Enforcement reads the recorded verdict from the DB, never the exit code, so nothing lands through Claude Code. Their "CI steps" justification is also off batten's advertised surface — DESIGN.md line 43 explicitly deprioritizes headless/CI paths, `batten check` is not listed in `printUsage()`, and no skill or plugin file invokes it. The `&&`-chain half of their EXPECTED is sound; the CI half is not why this matters.

Net: a real, reproducible CLI-contract defect with a narrow but genuine failure mode (any shell or agent composition, plus a plain terminal outside Claude Code where no git pre-commit hook exists — batten installs none, so the exit code is the only signal there). It is a one-line fix. But it is not a gate bypass, so it is not the blocker the write-up implies. Minor, and worth fixing.

title: `evidence: [""]` satisfies the evidence rule — the guard counts items, not content
reason:
Reproduced verbatim, and the source confirms it: `internal/store/store.go:598` is `if evidenceRequired && v.Result == "ok" && len(v.Evidence) == 0`. There is no `TrimSpace`, no empty-item filter, anywhere between `json.Unmarshal` in `cmd/batten/main.go:250` and the INSERT. `[""]` has len 1, so it passes. Same count-only test is repeated at `cmd/batten/main.go:707` (the `close` path), `internal/hooks/hooks.go:312` (the commit gate) and `internal/mcp/mcp.go:476`. The reporter's EXPECTED is correct in direction: this is not one of batten's deliberate looks-like-a-bug behaviours (fail-open-with-warning, advisory-not-deny, unmeasurable-not-zero). Rejecting a string that is empty after trimming is not a content judgement — it is unambiguous input normalization, and README:48 states the rule as "an approval must cite something", which `""` does not. ROADMAP:34 lists under *Verified*: "An envelope with an empty `evidence[]` is refused by the binary before it reaches the database" — a reader takes "empty evidence" to mean "cites nothing", and this reaches the database.

Where the finding is overstated, and why I am correcting severity to **minor** rather than letting it stand as a gate bypass:

1. **It never opened the commit gate in a spec whose gate declares `checks`.** With `gates.qa.checks` present (as in every shipped example and as the docs mandate), the `PreToolUse` hook still denied after I recorded `evidence:[""]`: `"batten: US-011 has no batten-verified pass. The gate's checks must be RUN, not asserted. Run: batten check US-011"`. The second layer at `hooks.go:328` — demanding a `source="batten"` verdict — is the actual teeth, and it is untouched by this.
2. **In the only config where it does slip through (a gate with no `checks`), batten already labels the approval as worthless.** The hook returned a standing warning: `"gate \"qa\" declares no checks, so US-012 was approved on the agent's word alone — nothing was run to verify it."`
3. **It grants an adversarial agent nothing new.** `evidence:["tests pass"]` is equally hollow, equally accepted, and equally impossible to mechanize — the `batten-verdict` SKILL.md explicitly forbids `"tests pass"` in prose precisely because the binary cannot check it. Fixing `[""]` raises the bar from "type nothing" to "type one character". Real hygiene; not a security boundary.

The genuine, non-cosmetic consequence I found beyond what was reported: `batten close US-011 --status ok` **succeeded** on this verdict (exit 0, `runs` now shows `US-011 ok ok`) even in the checks-bearing spec where the commit hook denies — so the run ledger, and any exported run note, records a unit closed `ok` citing nothing. That is the part worth fixing, and it is a one-line fix at `store.go:598` plus the three mirrored call sites.

title: report mode still tells you to run an override for something it did not block
reason:
Reproducible verbatim, but it is not a defect — it is the documented design, and the reporter's EXPECTED is wrong on the merits.

1. The output does NOT mislead the user about blocking. The same payload's user-visible line is `"batten (warning — not blocking): ..."`. The escape-hatch sentence lives only in `additionalContext` (the model's context), not in the `systemMessage` banner — `advise()` in internal/hooks/hooks.go:108 deliberately passes the reason through `firstLine()` for the banner and the full text to the model.

2. The suggested override is NOT a no-op in report mode. I ran it. `batten override US-015 --reason "..."` records the override and the very next PreToolUse hook returns empty output — the warning stops. In report mode the gate warns on EVERY `git commit`, and the override is the only way to say "I know, stop telling me" while leaving it on the record. The reporter's primary fix (drop the line) would delete a working, audited affordance.

3. The reporter's proposed replacement text is backwards. Telling a user whose commit just warned that the remedy is "flip enforcement: enforce in batten.yaml to make this a denial" advises them to make the gate stricter as the cure for a warning. Nobody wants that.

4. Identical reason text across modes is the point of report mode, not an oversight. ROADMAP.md:101 frames report as the adoption ramp — gates "start at `enforcement: report` ... and harden to `enforce` when the team trusts them." Report mode is a dress rehearsal for enforce; showing exactly the text enforce will show, escape hatch included, is what makes the rehearsal informative. `gate()` (hooks.go:98) is explicitly written as "same reason, different consequence." Rewriting the reason per mode would break the preview. This is squarely one of the "deliberate behaviours that LOOK like bugs."

Residual truth worth exactly one word of polish: "To proceed anyway" reads oddly when nothing stopped you. That is a wording nit inside a message the user never sees in full, not a gap or a break.

ADJACENT — three things I hit while testing that are MORE substantive than the finding under review, all personally reproduced, and none of which the reporter noticed:
(a) `batten show US-015` prints "no verdict: the close gate will deny a commit" while enforcement is `report` AND after an override was recorded. That is flatly false on two counts — the strong version of the complaint the reporter filed against the weak case.
(b) `batten override` prints "the gate will now allow the commit" in report mode, where the gate was already allowing it.
(c) An override taken during report mode survives hardening to enforce: I recorded the override under `report`, flipped `enforcement` back to `enforce`, re-ran the hook, and it allowed the commit with no output. So the nudge in (the reviewed) message can, in principle, plant a stale bypass that outlives the ramp. Defensible — overrides are per run+gate and auditable by design — but (a) is a real copy defect that should be filed instead of this one.

reason:
Reproduced byte-for-byte in a fresh sandbox, and the reporter's diagnosis of the cause is correct — but the severity should be read as a diagnostics/message defect, not an enforcement defect.

WHAT IS TRUE. At $HOME/Proyectos/Public/LoopWorkFlow/internal/hooks/hooks.go:328-336 the gate does:

    bv, err := h.Store.LatestVerdictBySource(run.RunID, gateName, "batten")
    if err != nil || bv.Result != "ok" {
        return h.gate("PreToolUse", fmt.Sprintf(
            "batten: %s has no batten-verified pass. The gate's checks must be RUN, not asserted.\n"+
            "Run: batten check %s\n" ...

Two materially different states collapse into one string: (a) no batten verdict exists at all, and (b) a batten verdict exists and says the checks FAILED. I drove both and got identical messages modulo the unit id (US-011 = checks ran and failed; US-012 = checks never ran). `bv` is fetched and then discarded — `bv.Why` ("one or more gate checks failed") and `bv.Evidence` ("python -m pytest backend/tests -q: FAIL (exit 4)" plus 8 lines of tail, which I confirmed is physically in the DB) are already in hand at that line, at zero extra query cost. So the reporter's EXPECTED message is not a wish; it is constructible from the variable the code already holds.

The remediation line is also wrong in the failing case: it tells you to run `batten check <unit>`, which is exactly what you already did.

The branch is inconsistent with batten's own established pattern. The sibling branch 10 lines above (hooks.go:318-322) does surface `v.Why` and `v.SafeNextStep`, and the branch above that names the phase to run. This one branch, holding the richest information of the three, prints the least.

WHY THE REPORTER IS NOT WRONG ABOUT DESIGN. I checked README.md, DESIGN.md, ROADMAP.md for a deliberate behaviour this could be mistaken for. This is not one of them — it is not the fail-open-with-warning path (that is the no-checks-declared `advise()` at hooks.go:347, a different branch), not the advisory-write path, and not the unmeasurable-vs-zero reporting rule. DESIGN.md:403 argues the opposite way: "Un verdict gate que bloquea mal es peor que no tenerlo" — a gate must be legible to survive. Nothing in the docs asks for a terse denial.

WHY IT IS NOT WORSE THAN MINOR. The decision batten makes is exactly right and I verified all three arms:
- agent writes ok on top of a failed batten check -> DENY. The dishonest-approval hole stays closed.
- checks genuinely fixed and re-run -> gate opens (empty hook output, allow).
So the headline promise — "the gate's checks must be RUN, not asserted" — is delivered. Nothing ships that should not. The cost of the bad message is bounded: one re-run of `batten check`, which prints the failures loudly and ends with "the commit gate will deny until this passes." The agent is not going to loop forever.

Two things push it to the top of minor rather than polish. First, the recommended next step is affirmatively misleading, not merely vague. Second, the obvious investigative command reinforces the confusion: `batten show US-011` in the failing state prints only "verdict qa=ok (agent)" with its three cited lines and shows no trace whatsoever of the batten-produced BLOCKED verdict. A user denied at the gate, told to run a check they already ran, who then inspects the run, sees a green ok and no failure anywhere. The failing evidence is stored but reachable by no command except re-running the check.

ONE INACCURACY IN THE REPORT, immaterial: the EXPECTED text cites "exit 1". Real pytest exit here is 4 (no tests collected). That is the reporter illustrating a message shape, not misreporting an observation.
